routines.name: _id_list
routines.docstring:
Read an optional array of change IDs, rejecting anything malformed.

`depends_on` and the caller-supplied `applied` journal both arrive as lists
of IDs. A non-array, or an element that is not a nonempty string, is broken
input rather than a graph problem, so both raise `code`
("invalid-change"). Duplicates inside the list carry no meaning and are
collapsed so membership tests against `applied` stay exact.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate change records and collapse identical duplicates.

Duplicates are compared on id, component, units and the *set* of
dependencies; order inside `depends_on` is not identity. One record per ID
survives. Records that share an ID but differ in any of those fields are a
conflict, not a merge: silently keeping one would change what gets
deployed, so they fail with `conflicting-change`.

journal.py.moduleNote:

This module owns input validation, change identity and replay state. It is the

routines.name: ordered_ids
routines.docstring:
Return the full deterministic topological order of all change IDs.

Dependencies that are already applied do not hold a change back: replay
means the persisted journal satisfies them. Ties among currently eligible
changes are broken by lexicographic ID so the same request always yields
the same order. If anything never becomes eligible a cycle exists;
reporting it here keeps plan and rollback consistent, because rollback
needs the full order even though it emits only a subset.

comments: # Unknown IDs are checked before ordering: a dependency on a change that
# was never supplied, or an applied ID that disappears from the request,
# is a journal/data problem, not a cycle.
# Budget is checked against the emitted units, after replay and
# deduplication, so already-applied changes never consume new capacity.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Planner is the only module that sees the whole request: it asks journal for

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Validate environment, action and budget; return the budget.

G1 supports plan and rollback in both environments. A missing or unknown
action is `unsupported-action`, not a default, so an undefined operation can
never fall back into a plan. `budget` is always validated here, and the
value is returned so planner can apply it per action: it caps plan only.

routines.name: check_budget
routines.docstring:
Enforce the spend cap for the action being emitted.

Only plan spends new capacity, so only plan can exceed the budget. Rollback
retires already-applied changes; capping it would leave a release stuck
rolled halfway, so its validated budget is deliberately not applied here.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Read the persisted release journal (`applied`) supplied by the caller.

Membership in this list is what makes a change already deployed for replay;
membership tests therefore live with the rest of the identity data here.
The field defaults to empty only when it is absent; an explicit null is
malformed (`invalid-change`) like any other non-array.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Read the G2 `retain` list for a staging rollback.

`retain` names applied changes the caller wants left in place; the default
is empty, i.e. a plain rollback. It is rollback-only: planner never reads it
for a plan, so a stray `retain` on a plan cannot alter the emitted actions.

Unlike `depends_on`/`applied`, malformed input here is `invalid-retain`, a
distinct code, because it is a rollback-specific argument and the caller
needs to tell it apart from a broken change record. Any ID that is not in
the persisted journal is rejected too: retaining something that was never
applied would silently keep a phantom, so it is a caller mistake.

The cross-check against `applied` lives here so planner gets a clean,
already-validated set and only has to decide the dependency closure.
Defaulting mirrors the other lists: absent means empty, explicit null is
malformed and stays `invalid-retain`.

routines.name: ordered_ids

routines.name: retained_ids
routines.docstring:
Expand `retain` into the applied IDs a rollback must leave in place.

A retained change is useless without its prerequisites, so the set is the
*transitive* dependency closure of the retained IDs, restricted to changes
that are actually applied: an unapplied dependency is not running and
therefore needs no retention. Only applied changes can be emitted by
rollback at all, so anything outside `applied` is irrelevant here.

`retain` itself is already validated (applied membership, shape) by journal;
this function adds only the graph walk. The closure terminates because a
cycle was already rejected before this point.

# never be influenced by it. Validation happens before the walk, and
# kept IDs are subtracted from the reverse order rather than

Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Validate environment, action and budget; return the effective budget.

This is the first policy gate planner calls, before reading changes or the
journal. Order matters for two G2 rules:

* This release is staging-only. A `production` request is frozen for both
  plan and rollback and is rejected here, before any graph or change
  validation, so even a malformed graph in production reports
  `production-frozen` rather than `invalid-change`/`dependency-cycle`.
  The environment itself is still validated first: an unknown value stays
  `invalid-environment`.
* The returned budget is what plan is capped by: on staging it is the
  smaller of the request budget and `STAGING_PLAN_QUOTA`. The request value
  is still validated in full (`invalid-budget`) so a malformed field is
  reported even when the quota would be the tighter bound.

A missing or unknown action is `unsupported-action`, not a default, so an
undefined operation can never fall back into a plan.

Both comparisons use `isinstance(..., str)` first: a JSON array or object
is unhashable and would raise TypeError inside a set/`in` test, escaping as
a crashed process instead of the error object this service promises to
always print.

routines.name: check_budget
routines.docstring:
Enforce the spend cap for the action being emitted.

Only plan spends new capacity, so only plan can exceed the budget; for
staging plans that budget is already quota-capped by `limit_for`, so the
quota violation surfaces as the same `budget-exceeded`. Rollback retires
already-applied changes; capping it would leave a release stuck rolled
halfway, so its validated budget is deliberately not applied here.

# spend rule, and planner must stay unaware of policy numbers.

# so no other validation error should mask the real reason for refusal.

routines.name: _string_list
routines.docstring:
Return ``row[key]`` as a list of strings; ``None`` means "absent".

A key present with value ``null`` is malformed, not absent: the host's
transport contract pins ``depends_on: null`` to invalid-change, and
defaulting it would silently accept a record whose author meant something
else. A missing key is the only way to request the empty default.
Only lists of nonempty strings are accepted. A bare string would otherwise
be iterated character by character and silently turn "ab" into ["a", "b"],
so it is rejected instead of coerced.

routines.name: _record
routines.docstring:
Validate one change record and return it with a canonical dependency set.

``depends_on`` is stored sorted and de-duplicated because record identity
is defined by the *set* of dependencies: two records that only differ in
dependency order (or repeat a dependency) are the same change, not a
conflict.

routines.name: read_changes
routines.docstring:
Validate ``changes`` and collapse identical duplicates.

Returns records in first-appearance order. The order does not affect the
result (the planner sorts by ID), but it keeps diagnostics reproducible.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring:
Validate the persisted journal and return it as a set of change IDs.

Use :func:`read_optional_applied` for the request field: a present ``null``
is malformed there, while this function only sees an already-vetted list.

routines.name: read_optional_applied
routines.docstring:
Read an optional list-of-strings field, distinguishing absent from null.

``None`` meant two different things in an early version of this module
(absent key and JSON ``null``), which silently accepted ``"applied": null``.
The host's transport contract pins a present ``null`` to ``invalid-change``,
so the two cases must be separated at the boundary, not deeper down.

routines.name: check_references
routines.docstring:
Reject unknown dependency targets and unknown applied IDs.

Applied IDs are checked against the same change graph, so a journal entry
for a change that is no longer described by the request is treated as a
broken reference rather than ignored.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Kahn's algorithm with lexicographic ID tie-breaking.

Uses a heap over currently eligible IDs, so the order is uniquely
determined by the ID set and the dependency relation -- it never depends
on the input order or on dict/set iteration order.

The sweep is iterative on purpose: a deep chain of thousands of changes
must not hit Python's recursion limit.

plan: unapplied changes in topological order; bill the sum of their units,

rollback: applied changes in the reverse of the *full* topological order.

      not-yet-applied one, and reversing only the applied sub-sequence
      would emit a dependency after its dependent. Rollback ignores budget.

# node on a cycle (or downstream of one) keeps a positive in-degree, so a short
# result is exactly "a cycle exists". A self-dependency is just the 1-ring case.
# Push only when the node becomes eligible, which is what makes
# "lexicographically smallest among *currently* eligible" hold.
# Every node on a cycle (and everything downstream of it) keeps a
# positive in-degree, so a short fall automatically means a cycle.
# Non-object input (array, string, null, number) is a transport-level
# problem, reported before any field could be inspected.

# for plan. The whole request fails rather than emitting a prefix.

routines.name: authorize
routines.docstring:
Validate environment, action and budget; return ``(action, budget)``.

The order of the three checks is part of the contract, because it decides
which code wins when a request is wrong in several ways at once:

* ``environment`` first, so a non-string or unknown value is

* ``action`` next: an unknown operation is ``unsupported-action``, never a
  silent fallback to plan.
* ``production-frozen`` next, and before the *caller* reads any change.
  CHANGE-G2 pins that a production request reports the freeze even when the
  graph is malformed, so this must run before budget/change validation.

  ``budget: true`` on a production request is ``production-frozen``.
* ``budget`` last: ``type(...) is int`` excludes booleans on purpose
  (``True`` is an int in Python but is not a valid budget).

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the effective budget for an already-authorized request.

G2: a staging plan is capped by ``STAGING_PLAN_QUOTA``, so the effective
budget is ``min(budget, 3)``. A quota violation therefore surfaces as the
ordinary ``budget-exceeded`` raised by the planner's comparison, not as a
separate code; the request budget is still validated in full above so a
malformed value is reported even when the quota would be the tighter bound.

Only ``plan`` is capped. Rollback retires already-applied changes; capping
it would leave a release stuck rolled halfway, so its (validated) budget is
returned unchanged and never compared against emitted units.

`invalid-retain` rather than `invalid-change`, so the caller can tell which
field was wrong.

`None` is treated as absent (the empty list) because an explicit JSON null
arrives here as None on an optional field; it must behave like an omitted
key rather than inventing an error.

matching the existing rule that unknown extra fields are ignored.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:

routines.name: retained_closure
routines.docstring:
IDs that a staging rollback must keep: `retain` plus its applied deps.

G2-3: the caller names already-applied changes that must stay; their
transitive dependencies must stay too, otherwise the release journal would
end up with a change whose dependency was rolled back.

Non-obvious boundaries:
- A `retain` ID that is not applied is `invalid-retain`. An applied ID that
  does not exist at all never reaches here: `known()` already reported it as
  `unknown-dependency`, keeping G1's precedence for a broken journal. G2
  adds a check for a *well-formed but wrong* journal, it does not reorder G1.
- The closure also requires every dependency it walks to be applied. If a
  retained change depends on a change the journal never recorded, keeping
  the dependent would leave the journal inconsistent (it would claim an
  applied change whose dependency is gone), so it is `invalid-retain` rather
  than a silently partial keep.
- Iterative BFS, not recursion: dependency chains can be thousands deep
  (see the deep-chain test) and would exceed the default recursion limit.

routines.name: limit_for

Return the effective budget, or raise the environment/action/budget error.

  budgets being checked first, and G2 supersedes it for production.
- It still runs after the environment check: an unknown environment is not
  production and must keep reporting `invalid-environment` (G1 behaviour).
